explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. God says the opposite: “As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, you will no longer quote this proverb in Israel.” (Ezekiel 18:3) That proverb is getting hung up like an apron at closing time. It's done.

That's it, baker. God says, “As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, you will no longer quote this proverb in Israel.” (Ezekiel 18:3) He puts His own life behind those words. The sour grapes saying is finished.
Right on the money, baker. God says, “…every soul belongs to Me; both father and son are Mine.” (Ezekiel 18:4) So the souls in this story were never anybody else's to trade around. They're His.

Fathers get a lot of credit, friend, but not this one. God says, “both father and son are Mine.” (Ezekiel 18:4) A dad doesn't hold the deed to his kids' souls, and neither does a son hold one to his dad's.

The king of Babylon, a foreign king, can wear whatever crown he likes, and it still won't get him this. God says, “…every soul belongs to Me…” (Ezekiel 18:4) That covers both father and son. No king is mentioned anywhere in that verse.
Yes, baker. God says, “The soul who sins is the one who will die.” (Ezekiel 18:4) Each soul answers for its own sin. That's the opposite of the sour grapes saying.

Careful, friend, that's the old proverb talking. God says it plainly later: “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father…” (Ezekiel 18:20) The soul who sins is the one who dies. Dad's sin doesn't land on a son's plate.

Close, but it doesn't go that way either. God says, “…a father will not bear the iniquity of his son.” (Ezekiel 18:20) Right before that, He says, “The soul who sins is the one who will die.” (Ezekiel 18:20)

That's the one, baker. The righteous man “…gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing.” (Ezekiel 18:7) He sees people in need and he hands over what he has. Bread and clothing are just part of how he lives, because God's list goes on.
Power isn't who the verse names, friend. It says he “…gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing.” (Ezekiel 18:7) The ones he gives to are the hungry and the naked.

That one sounds like a networking lunch, friend. The verse says he “…gives his bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing.” (Ezekiel 18:7) The people on the receiving end are the hungry and the naked. Nobody's handing out business cards here.

Right, baker. God says of him, “That man is righteous; surely he will live, declares the Lord GOD.” (Ezekiel 18:9) He follows God's statutes and faithfully keeps His ordinances. And God says he will live.

Not this time, friend. God says, “That man is righteous; surely he will live, declares the Lord GOD.” (Ezekiel 18:9) The man follows His statutes and keeps His ordinances faithfully. So the answer is a clear yes: he lives.

I get the thought, friend. A righteous dad is a blessing, but his record doesn't transfer. God asks, “Will this son live? He will not!” (Ezekiel 18:13) Because of his own abominations, “…he will surely die; his blood will be on his own head.” (Ezekiel 18:13) You can't hand your good name down like an old recipe card.

You got it, baker. God asks about the violent son, “Will this son live? He will not!” (Ezekiel 18:13) The text ties his death to “…all these abominations…” his own, and nothing about his father's goodness changes that. His father's righteous life doesn't carry him.

explanations.answer: Thinks it over and does not copy it
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. He “…sees all the sins his father has committed, considers them, and does not do likewise…” (Ezekiel 18:14) He looks, he thinks, and he walks a different way. A front-row seat doesn't mean he has to join the show.

explanations.answer: Copies his father one sin at a time
explanations.explanation: That's what his father did, friend. But the text says this son “…does not do likewise…” (Ezekiel 18:14) He sees the sins, considers them, and doesn't repeat them.

explanations.answer: Tries to make up for it with offerings
explanations.explanation: Offerings aren't mentioned here, friend. The text says he sees his father's sins, considers them, and “…does not do likewise…” (Ezekiel 18:14) Then it lists what he does: he doesn't look to idols, he gives his bread to the hungry, and he keeps God's ordinances (Ezekiel 18:15-17).

That's right, baker. God says of the father, “…he will die for his own iniquity, because he practiced extortion, robbed his brother, and did what was wrong among his people.” (Ezekiel 18:18) The son's good choices belong to the son. Each one stands on his own.

I see why you'd hope so, friend, but the text says otherwise. God says of the father, “…he will die for his own iniquity…” (Ezekiel 18:18) The son doing right means the son lives, but it doesn't erase his father's sin. Everybody answers for their own.

explanations.answer: He did what is just and right
explanations.explanation: That's the answer, baker. God says, “Since the son has done what is just and right, carefully observing all My statutes, he will surely live.” (Ezekiel 18:19) His life is tied to what he did. Nothing about it depends on his father.

explanations.answer: He moved away from his father
explanations.explanation: That's a creative guess, friend, but the text never mentions anybody moving. It says he lives “Since the son has done what is just and right, carefully observing all My statutes…” (Ezekiel 18:19) Distance wasn't the point. His own choices were.

Nobody's covering his tab, friend. The text says his father “…will die for his own iniquity…” (Ezekiel 18:18) The son lives because “…the son has done what is just and right…” (Ezekiel 18:19) His own choices carry him, not his dad's.

You got it, baker. “The righteousness of the righteous man will fall upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked man will fall upon him.” (Ezekiel 18:20) It lands on the one who did it, and on nobody else. That's why a son isn't stuck with his father's sin.

That's the old sour grapes thinking, friend. But God says, “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son.” (Ezekiel 18:20) The righteousness or wickedness falls “upon him,” the one who did it. The family line doesn't carry it.

No group blame here, friend. God says the righteousness of the righteous man and the wickedness of the wicked man each fall “upon him.” (Ezekiel 18:20) That means one person at a time. Nobody gets dragged along for somebody else's sin.

That would be a heavy load to carry, friend, but God says otherwise. If the wicked man turns from all his sins and does what is just and right, “…he will surely live; he will not die.” (Ezekiel 18:21) And “None of the transgressions he has committed will be held against him.” (Ezekiel 18:22) His old sins don't come back around.

Yes, baker, and that is a lot of good news. God says, “…he will surely live; he will not die.” (Ezekiel 18:21) “None of the transgressions he has committed will be held against him.” (Ezekiel 18:22) When he turns, his past isn't held against him.

explanations.answer: That he turns from his ways and lives
explanations.explanation: That's God's own heart on the matter, baker. He asks, “Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23) He asks it right after asking if He takes any pleasure in the death of the wicked. The answer He's pointing to is no.

explanations.answer: That he pays for every one of his sins
explanations.explanation: That's not how God puts it, friend. He asks, “Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23) And earlier He says that when the wicked man turns, none of his transgressions “…will be held against him.” (Ezekiel 18:22) The whole point is life.

explanations.answer: That he stays far away from Israel
explanations.explanation: Nobody's getting sent away in this verse, friend. God asks, “Wouldn’t I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23) What He wants is for the man to turn and live. Where he lives doesn't come up.

explanations.answer: None of them will be remembered
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. God says, “None of the righteous acts he did will be remembered.” (Ezekiel 18:24) Turning away to the same abominations as the wicked takes a man's past good deeds off the table. It's a sobering verse, and I think it's a loving warning to keep going.

explanations.answer: They cancel out his new sins
explanations.explanation: That would be convenient, friend. But God says the opposite: “None of the righteous acts he did will be remembered.” (Ezekiel 18:24) And “Because of the unfaithfulness and sin he has committed, he will die.” (Ezekiel 18:24)

explanations.answer: They protect his children from harm
explanations.explanation: The verse never brings his children into it, friend. It says, “None of the righteous acts he did will be remembered.” (Ezekiel 18:24) And earlier God says that the righteousness of the righteous man falls upon him. (Ezekiel 18:20) The man's own record is what's at stake here.

That's a kind hope, friend, but God asks, “…will he live?” and then answers, “Because of the unfaithfulness and sin he has committed, he will die.” (Ezekiel 18:24) Past righteousness doesn't keep a man alive if he turns to the same abominations as the wicked. He has to keep going the right way.

That's it, baker. God asks, “…will he live?” and gives the answer: “Because of the unfaithfulness and sin he has committed, he will die.” (Ezekiel 18:24) Turning to the abominations of the wicked is what costs him. A good start doesn't cover a turn like that.

You've got it, baker. The people say, “The way of the Lord is not just.” God answers, “Is it My way that is unjust? Is it not your ways that are unjust?” (Ezekiel 18:25) He hands the question right back to them. It's like handing someone the mirror.

He does turn it around, friend. After the people say, “The way of the Lord is not just.” God asks, “Is it My way that is unjust? Is it not your ways that are unjust?” (Ezekiel 18:25) The question comes straight back to them. That's what the verse says.
That's right, baker. God says, “…I will judge you, each according to his ways…” (Ezekiel 18:30) One person at a time, by what they did. It matches everything we just heard.

explanations.answer: By the deeds of their kings
explanations.explanation: Kings don't get the spotlight in this verse, friend. God says, “…I will judge you, each according to his ways…” (Ezekiel 18:30) That's about each person's own ways. Nobody gets judged by somebody else's record.

God speaks to the whole house of Israel, but He doesn't judge them in one lump. He says, “…I will judge you, each according to his ways…” (Ezekiel 18:30) Each one, by his own ways. Nobody gets lost in the crowd, and nobody gets blamed for the crowd.

explanations.answer: So their iniquity won't be their downfall
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. God says, “Repent and turn from all your transgressions, so that your iniquity will not become your downfall.” (Ezekiel 18:30) The call to turn comes with a reason, and the reason is that they don't fall. I think that's a Father pointing out the open door.

explanations.answer: So the priests will accept their offerings
explanations.explanation: Priests and offerings aren't in this verse, friend. God says, “Repent and turn from all your transgressions, so that your iniquity will not become your downfall.” (Ezekiel 18:30) The reason given is about their downfall, and nothing else.

explanations.answer: So their enemies will leave them alone
explanations.explanation: Enemies don't show up here, friend. The reason God gives is this: “…so that your iniquity will not become your downfall.” (Ezekiel 18:30) The danger He names is their own iniquity. That's what He's telling them to turn from.

That's the one, baker. God says, “Cast away from yourselves all the transgressions you have committed…” (Ezekiel 18:31) Throw them out, every last one. Think of sweeping crumbs off the counter instead of saving them for later.

Keeping a scorecard sounds organized, friend, but God says the opposite. “Cast away from yourselves all the transgressions you have committed…” (Ezekiel 18:31) He tells them to throw them away, not file them. No notebook needed.

The priests aren't in this verse, friend. God says, “Cast away from yourselves all the transgressions you have committed…” (Ezekiel 18:31) The command is to cast them away, plain and simple. Then He adds the new heart and new spirit.
